title: Freya and the Letter
premise: In 1792, in a river city on the brink of revolution, Rafael Fairweather works as a compositor and courier for her father's print shop, moving forbidden pamphlets through checkpoints that search everything but paper. When an infant is abandoned at the shop door with a letter naming names—evidence that could hang half the neighborhood—Rafael must choose between the anonymity that has kept her family alive and the child no one will claim. Over one winter she builds a fragile found family around the girl, smuggles the letter past three checkpoints, and finally trades her own silence to a sympathetic magistrate, exposing the conspirators at the cost of the print shop itself. The book ends with Rafael, dispossessed but unbroken, carrying the child across the frozen river toward a new life as the old century dies.
about_author: Rosalind Yarrow is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing printers' ledgers and broadsides from the revolutionary era. She writes from a converted bindery on the coast, where she still sets type by hand.

chapters.title: The Weight of Lead
chapters.summary: Rafael Fairweather introduces her world: the print shop, her father's failing eyesight, and the city's rising unrest. In her POV, we learn she measures survival in what can be carried. She delivers seditious pamphlets past a bored checkpoint guard. Emotional beat: quiet competence masking fear.

chapters.title: Instructions to Forget
chapters.summary: A hooded woman leaves an infant at the shop door before dawn with a sealed letter and coins, whispering instructions to forget her face. Rafael, POV, hides the child from a surprise inspection. Emotional beat: the first crack in her practiced invisibility.

chapters.title: What the Letter Said
chapters.summary: Rafael and her father read the letter: names of conspirators, including men who protect the shop. Burning it would be safest; keeping it is leverage and death sentence both. Father's POV reveals his own buried guilt. Emotional beat: dread of knowledge.

chapters.title: Naming the Child
chapters.summary: Against all sense, Rafael keeps the baby, calling her Wren. The shop's apprentice, Tomas, becomes a reluctant co-conspirator. His POV shows his fear of Rafael's recklessness—and his growing devotion. Emotional beat: found family taking root.

chapters.title: First Checkpoint: The Bridge
chapters.summary: Rafael attempts to move the letter sewn into a returned book, but the bridge checkpoint tightens under new martial orders. She turns back, nearly caught when Wren cries. Her POV. Emotional beat: the cost of hesitation.

chapters.title: The Magistrate Who Reads
chapters.summary: Magistrate Corvane, who buys books from the shop, notices Rafael's distraction and probes gently. Their cat-and-mouse conversation suggests he may not be the enemy. His POV hints at private doubts about the regime. Emotional beat: dangerous hope.

chapters.title: Someone Is Asking After Faces
chapters.summary: A government agent, Hessler, arrives asking about a woman with a child—the mother was caught and talked. Rafael lies fluently while inside she panics. Tomas's POV watches her lie and realizes how far she'll go. Emotional beat: terror sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Second Checkpoint: The Custom House
chapters.summary: Rafael hides the letter inside a shipment of type molds bound downriver. The custom house search strips the crate; only Tomas's quick forgery of shipping papers saves them. Dual POV tension. Emotional beat: victory that feels like a warning.

chapters.title: Winter Takes the Shop
chapters.summary: Fuel runs short; the father falls ill. Rafael sells type to buy medicine, weakening the business that hides them all. Her POV grapples with trading future for present. Emotional beat: the price of survival made literal.

chapters.title: Hessler's Offer
chapters.summary: Hessler corners Rafael privately: give him the letter and the names, and the shop stays open. He suspects her; he simply can't prove it yet. Her POV calculates betrayal against exposure. Emotional beat: temptation wearing a polite face.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Knew
chapters.summary: Old Marta, the dyer next door, reveals she recognized the mother months ago and has been leaving milk at the door. Marta's POV opens the neighborhood's silent web of complicity. Emotional beat: loneliness dissolving into community.

chapters.title: Third Checkpoint: The Gate of Ashes
chapters.summary: Rafael passes the final checkpoint disguised as a mourning widow, the letter hidden in a funeral wreath. She reaches the safe contact—only to find his house raided hours before. Her POV. Emotional beat: hope collapsing at the threshold.

chapters.title: What Tomas Did
chapters.summary: Tomas confesses he copied the letter weeks ago and sent word to a printer's underground network, trying to help. Rafael rages at the risk, then realizes the copy changes everything. His POV, shame and stubborn love. Emotional beat: anger transmuting into trust.

chapters.title: The Raid
chapters.summary: Soldiers raid the print shop at night. The father is taken for questioning; the press is smashed. Rafael escapes with Wren through the cellar into Marta's care. Her POV, dissociated with shock. Emotional beat: everything carried, nothing left to carry it in.

chapters.title: Corvane's Choice
chapters.summary: Magistrate Corvane is assigned to prosecute the father. His POV wrestles between career and conscience as he recognizes the case is theater staged by Hessler. Emotional beat: a good man measuring his soul.

chapters.title: Bargaining in the Dark
chapters.summary: Rafael approaches Corvane secretly with the truth—not to beg, but to deal: testimony for her father's release. Their negotiation crackles with mutual recognition. Alternating POV. Emotional beat: justice outside the law begins here.

chapters.title: The Trial of Typesetters
chapters.summary: The father stands trial amid manufactured evidence. Corvane dismantles Hessler's case using the letter's contents, forcing the conspiracy into the open. Courtroom scene, mostly Corvane's POV. Emotional beat: the law briefly bending toward right.

chapters.title: Hessler's Reckoning
chapters.summary: Exposed, Hessler tries to seize Wren as leverage, believing the child is proof of treason. Rafael confronts him publicly in the square, and the crowd—her neighborhood—closes ranks around her. Her POV. Emotional beat: invisible no longer.

chapters.title: Ashes of the Press
chapters.summary: The shop is forfeit regardless; the regime punishes the district. The father, freed but broken, tells Rafael to go where he cannot follow. Bittersweet farewell scene, his POV. Emotional beat: love expressed as letting go.

chapters.title: The Century Turns
chapters.summary: On New Year's Eve, bells ring and rumors of revolution spread street to street. Rafael, Tomas, Marta, and Wren prepare to cross the frozen river. Her POV reflects on the year measured in what they carried. Emotional beat: grief and hope in the same breath.

chapters.title: Crossing
chapters.summary: The ice crossing at dawn, checkpoints behind them, soldiers' lanterns on the far bank. A moment where the ice groans and Wren laughs, unafraid. Rafael's POV, suspended between two lives. Emotional beat: terror and freedom indistinguishable.

chapters.title: Freya and the Letter
chapters.summary: On the far shore, Rafael burns the letter at last—its work done—and gives Wren a new name: Freya, after the goddess who survives every ending. Epilogue voice, years later, as Freya learns letters herself. Emotional beat: the story passed on, survival becoming inheritance.
